title: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal
goal: By the end you can remove shared changing state instead of locking it: build objects that never change, publish a new snapshot in one write, keep state on one thread, hand objects over through a queue, and use `ThreadLocal` without leaking one request's data into the next.
opening:
Picture the price board above a shop's counter. Ten customers can read it at once, and nobody takes turns, because nobody writes on it while they read. When prices change, the owner doesn't erase numbers while people read. She prints a new board and hangs it up in one move.

The shop's program usually does the opposite. It keeps the prices in a map that one thread updates in place while the threads at the tills (the cash registers) read it. (A thread is one path of work that runs side by side with others in the same program.) For a moment, a till can see the new price of bread next to the old price of milk. After ten lessons of tools, the habit is to add one more: a lock around the map.

Synchronizers made threads wait for each other. This lesson removes the reason to wait. We'll take a race apart into its two ingredients, sharing and change, and remove them one at a time: objects that never change, state only one thread can reach, and values each thread keeps for itself. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A record is Java's short form for a class whose fields are `final`. Take `record Quote(String item, List<String> tiers) {}`. A caller builds a quote from an `ArrayList` of price tiers, then adds one more tier to that same `ArrayList`. What does `quote.tiers()` show?
options: The original tiers only, because records are immutable
The new tier too, because the record holds the caller's list
It throws `UnsupportedOperationException` when the caller adds
It depends on whether the record was built with `new`
warmup.why: A record's fields are final, so `tiers` always points to the same list. But it's the caller's list, and nothing stops the caller from changing it. Records are only shallowly immutable. To make the quote really immutable, copy the list in a compact constructor with `List.copyOf`. The second section runs this with a bread quote.

sections.h: A race needs two ingredients: take away change with immutable snapshots

aside.title: Isn't a new object for every change slow?
aside.body: You may wonder whether building a whole new map for every refresh costs too much. For a price list that changes a few times an hour and is read thousands of times a second, it costs nothing you could measure. Making a small object in the JVM is cheap, often little more than moving a pointer, and short-lived objects are cheap to clean up. The JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code, can sometimes remove the new object altogether. Where it does hurt is data that changes millions of times a second, such as a hit counter, and for that an atomic from Atomics and compare-and-set fits better.

sections.h: Records and data classes freeze less than they seem: defensive copies

try.title: Change a record from outside
steps: Read `ShallowRecord`. `ShallowQuote` keeps the caller's list and array; `DeepQuote` copies them in and out. A third reference is an `unmodifiableList` view of the caller's list.
After construction, the caller changes its list and array, and a reader writes into the array it got from `signature()`. Predict all three lines.
Run it, then run the Kotlin twin, which adds one more line.

code.title: ShallowRecord.java

alt.title: ShallowRecord.kt
alt.src:
package workbench.concurrency.l11

// A data class's vals can't be reassigned. The objects they point to can still change.
private data class LooseQuote(val item: String, val tiers: List<String>, val signature: ByteArray)

private class SealedQuote(val item: String, tiers: List<String>, signature: ByteArray) {
    val tiers: List<String> = java.util.List.copyOf(tiers)    // copy in: unmodifiable even through a cast
    private val sig = signature.copyOf()
    val signature: ByteArray get() = sig.copyOf()             // copy out
}

fun main() {
    val tiers = mutableListOf("1 to 9 loaves at 2.50")
    val sig = byteArrayOf(7, 7, 7)
    val loose = LooseQuote("bread", tiers, sig)              // List<String> is read-only, not immutable
    val sealed = SealedQuote("bread", tiers, sig)
    val view = java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList(tiers)  // a read-only VIEW, not a copy

    tiers.add("10 or more at 0.01")                            // the caller keeps changing its list...
    sig[0] = 0                                                // ...and its array
    loose.signature[1] = 0                                    // a reader scribbles on what it was given
    sealed.signature[1] = 0

    println("shallow: ${loose.tiers}  signature ${loose.signature.contentToString()}")
    println("deep:    ${sealed.tiers}  signature ${sealed.signature.contentToString()}")
    println("unmodifiableList view: $view")
    (loose.tiers as MutableList<String>).add("added through a cast")   // read-only interface, mutable object
    println("shallow after a cast:  ${loose.tiers}")
}

try.expect: The shallow quote shows the extra tier and a signature of `[0, 0, 7]`: both the caller and a reader changed it. The deep quote still shows one tier and `[7, 7, 7]`. The `unmodifiableList` view shows the extra tier, because it's a view. In Kotlin, a cast to `MutableList` adds a line to the shallow quote's "read-only" list.

sections.h: Taking away sharing: confinement, and handing objects over
sections.body:
Changing state is fine as long as only one thread can reach it. That's **confinement**, keeping state where only one thread can get at it, and you already use it every day.

Stack confinement is the simplest kind. Local variables live on one thread's stack, its private list of method calls in progress, and no other thread can see them. A `StringBuilder` or `ArrayList` created inside a method and never stored anywhere else needs no protection at all:

```java
String receiptLine(Sale s) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();      // local: no other thread can ever see it
    sb.append(s.item()).append(';').append(s.cents());
    return sb.toString();                        // only the immutable String leaves
}
```

```kotlin
fun receiptLine(s: Sale): String = buildString {   // the builder is local: no other thread can see it
    append(s.item).append(';').append(s.cents)
}                                                  // only the immutable String leaves
```

Thread confinement is the same idea, made bigger. One thread owns some state, and every other thread asks that thread to act on it instead of touching the state itself. The mail-room helper from A thread's life worked this way: other parts of the program dropped messages into its tray, and only the helper ever sent them. Many screen toolkits work the same way, with one thread that is the only one allowed to draw on the screen.

When work has to move between threads, move the ownership with it. Back to the kitchen from wait, notify and guarded blocks: a waiter writes a ticket, clips it to the rail and never touches it again. The cook takes it and owns it from then on. In code, the rail is a `BlockingQueue`, the queue from Concurrent collections whose `take()` waits until something arrives:

```java
List<String> ticket = new ArrayList<>();         // owned by the waiter's thread
ticket.add("soup");
ticket.add("bread");
rail.put(ticket);                                // ownership moves to whoever takes it
// from here on, the waiter never touches ticket again
```

```kotlin
val ticket = ArrayList<String>()                 // owned by the waiter's thread
ticket.add("soup")
ticket.add("bread")
rail.put(ticket)                                 // ownership moves to whoever takes it
// from here on, the waiter never touches ticket again
```

The queue does two jobs. It hands the ticket over, and it makes the hand-over visible. Everything the waiter wrote before `put` happens-before the cook's `take` returns, so the cook sees the whole ticket. (Happens-before is the memory model's promise that one thread sees what another wrote first.) The figure shows the moment the owner changes.

The whole duty sits on the waiter's side: once you've handed something over, it isn't yours. Picture a waiter who saves paper by erasing a ticket the cook is still reading and writing the next table's order on it. The Try it does exactly that with `-Pargs=reuse`: the waiter clears one list and fills it again instead of making a new one. Each ticket holds 100 numbered dishes, so the cook can check that nothing is missing or out of order:

```text
new ticket each time: 5,000 tickets handed over, 0 damaged
one ticket, reused: 5,000 tickets handed over, 447 damaged
```

The reused ticket is a changing object shared by two threads with no synchronization at all, and the cook found 447 half-written tickets. Run it again and the number changes: runs here ranged from a few hundred to over 3,000. A lucky run could even show 0, which is exactly how this bug gets through testing.

**A queue hands over the object, not a copy. After put, never touch it again.**

Confinement keeps state on one thread. The last tool in this lesson does something stranger: it gives every thread its own copy of the same variable.

sections.h: One copy per thread: ThreadLocal, and why pool threads never forget

try.title: Watch one customer's context leak into another's request
steps: Read `ThreadLocalBleed`. Six requests run one after another on a pool of one thread. The handler sets the user only when the request carries one.
Predict what each request without a user runs as, in the leaky version and in the clean one.

code.title: ThreadLocalBleed.java

alt.title: ThreadLocalBleed.kt

try.expect: Leaky: the first anonymous request runs as `alice`, and the next two run as `bob`, whoever that thread served last. Clean: every anonymous request runs as `null`, because `remove()` in `finally` put the thread back as it was. A pool of one makes it happen every time. With 200 threads it happens rarely and at random, which is how it reaches real users.

compare.title: A deeply immutable value in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java record

kotlin.title: Kotlin class

compare.note: Both compile to a class with `final` fields, so both get the memory model's promise for final fields. The difference is where the copy can go. A Java record's compact constructor may reassign its parameters before the fields are set, so `lines = List.copyOf(lines)` stores the copy; that's Java doing the right thing with very little code. A Kotlin data class can't do the same, because its primary-constructor parameters are its properties. So you use a plain class with a separate property, as here, or a private constructor and a factory function. Kotlin's `List` type helps less than it looks: it's a read-only interface, and the results of `listOf` or `toList` can still be changed through a cast or from Java. `java.util.List.copyOf` gives you a list that is unmodifiable for everyone. A data class's `copy()` is shallow too: the copy shares the same list.

worked.title: A shared constant that someone changed

steps.say: The shop adds a delivery fee to every online order. `Money` looks like a value, and `DELIVERY_FEE` looks like a constant. Read it and find what changes, and for whom.

`add` changes the object it's called on, so `order.amount().add(DELIVERY_FEE)` changes the order's own amount. Somewhere else, `DELIVERY_FEE.add(surcharge)` changes the fee for every order on every thread. And because `cents` is neither `final` nor `volatile`, other threads may see the old fee, the new one, or a mix, at different times. `static final` on the reference didn't make the object constant.
Make `Money` a value: final fields, and operations that return a new object. Now 200 threads can read `DELIVERY_FEE` with no lock, and nobody can change it.

Before reading on, explain to yourself why the record needs no synchronization even though every request thread reads `DELIVERY_FEE`. Then look at the classic trap with immutable types, which catches everyone moving from changeable ones: calling the operation and throwing the result away.
steps.alt_code:
var total = BigDecimal.ZERO
for (fee in fees) total.add(fee)                 // does nothing: the result is thrown away
for (fee in fees) total += fee                   // right: plus() returns a new BigDecimal

steps.say: Answer: the fields are `final`, set once in the constructor, and the object never changes, so every thread that can see the reference sees 3.00 EUR. There's nothing to race on. The price is one new object per operation, which the JIT compiler often removes when the object never leaves the method. For money, that's an easy trade.

lab.title: A deeply immutable quote and a tenant scope that cleans up
steps: Meet the two classes. `FxQuote` is a price quote for changing money from one currency into another (FX is short for foreign exchange): a currency pair such as `EURUSD`, a list of price tiers and a signature, just like the bread quote in the second section. `TenantScope` carries the current tenant, the customer company a request works for, through one request on a pool thread, so deep code can ask `TenantScope.current()`.

Run the tests. All six fail. The three `FxQuote` tests change the quote from outside, through the list you passed in, the list it returns, and its signature array. The three `TenantScope` tests run on a pool of one thread and find a tenant left over from an earlier call.
Give `FxQuote` a compact constructor that replaces `tiers` with `List.copyOf(tiers)` and `signature` with a clone.
Override `signature()` so it returns a clone, not the field.

Fix `TenantScope.runAs`: remember the previous value, set the new one (or `remove()` for `null`), run the work in a `try`, and in `finally` put the previous value back (or `remove()` if there was none).
Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: In a compact constructor you assign to the parameter (`tiers = List.copyOf(tiers);`), not to `this.tiers`. The record sets the fields after your code runs.
`List.copyOf` also rejects `null` elements, which is usually what you want in a quote.
Putting back the previous value instead of always calling `remove()` makes nested calls work: an inner `runAs` must hand the thread back to the outer one, not wipe it.

drill.title: An immutable order from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an immutable `Order` with a customer name, a list of line items and a note, safe to share between threads, plus `withNote(String)` that returns a changed copy. Then check: can the caller's list, or the list you return, change your order?

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: A race needs state that is shared and changing. Take away either one, and there's nothing to lock.

An object nobody can change needs no locks: final fields, no setters, changing parts copied, and no `this` handed out before the constructor ends. For data that changes now and then, publish a new immutable snapshot with one write to a `volatile` field.
Records and data classes are shallow. Copy lists with `List.copyOf` and clone arrays on the way in and out; `unmodifiableList` is a view, not a copy.
Confinement keeps changing state on one thread: locals, one owner thread, or ownership handed through a queue and never touched again.
Every `ThreadLocal.set` on a pool thread needs a `remove()` in `finally`. On JDK 25 and later, scoped values do the cleanup for you.
The limit: state that is shared and changes by its nature, such as a balance, still needs a lock or an atomic.
closing:
We started with a price board that ten customers could read at once, because nobody wrote on it while they read. We gave the shop's program the same board, an immutable snapshot swapped in one write. Then we copied lists into records, handed tickets over for good, and cleaned up after every request.

Now search your own code for `ThreadLocal`. Every `set(` needs a `remove()` in a nearby `finally`, or a framework that clears it. Then look for records that keep a caller's list or array without copying it.

Some state can't be taken away. Next, we'll use the whole track's tools on three classic problems, starting with how a kitchen closes for the night without losing an order.

quiz.q: Which of these can be shared between threads with no synchronization at all?
options: A record whose `List<String>` component is the caller's `ArrayList`
A class with `volatile` fields and setters
A final class whose `private final` fields are a `String`, an `Instant` and a `BigDecimal`, with no setters
A record with an `int[]` component and the default accessor
quiz.why: All three field types are immutable and the fields are final, so the object can never change, and the promise for final fields makes it visible correctly. The record with the caller's list and the record with an array can both be changed from outside. `volatile` fields with setters make each write visible, but the object still changes under its readers.

quiz.q: A constructor stores `this.items = Collections.unmodifiableList(items);`. Later the caller adds an item to its own `items` list. What does the object's list show?
options: The original items only
It throws `UnsupportedOperationException` in the caller
The caller's add is ignored
The new item too, because `unmodifiableList` is a view of the caller's list
quiz.why: `unmodifiableList` only stops *you* from changing the list through that reference. It still reads the caller's list, so the caller's changes show through. `List.copyOf` makes a copy that nobody can change.

quiz.q: From Explicit locks: the shop's price list is replaced as a whole every 5 minutes and read 5,000 times a second. What is the simplest correct design?
options: A `ReentrantReadWriteLock` around a `HashMap`
A `volatile` field holding an immutable map, replaced with a freshly built `Map.copyOf(...)` on each refresh
A `ConcurrentHashMap` refreshed with `clear()` and `putAll()`
A `synchronized` getter and setter on a `HashMap`
quiz.why: Readers never wait, and each one sees one complete version, because the new map is built fully before one `volatile` write publishes it. The read-write lock also works, with more code and some cost on every read. `clear` plus `putAll` on a concurrent map lets readers see an empty or half-filled list.

quiz.q: A web service's request handler does `USER.set(request.user())` on a `ThreadLocal` when the request carries a user, and never removes it. Its threads come from a pool. What does a later anonymous request on the same thread see?
options: The previous request's user
`null`, because each request gets a fresh thread
An `IllegalStateException`
A random user from another thread
quiz.why: Pool threads are reused. The value stays on the thread until someone removes it, so the anonymous request runs as whoever that thread served last. Pair every `set` with `remove()` in `finally`.

quiz.q: A waiter thread puts an `ArrayList` ticket into a `BlockingQueue`, then calls `clear()` on the same list and fills it again for the next table. What does that do to the cook thread that takes it?
options: Nothing: `take()` returns a copy of the list
Nothing: `put` made the list thread-safe
The cook can see a partly cleared or refilled ticket, because the waiter kept changing an object it had handed over
`put` throws, because the list is already in the queue
quiz.why: The queue hands over a reference, not a copy. `put` happens-before `take` only for what the waiter did before the `put`. After that, the two threads share one changing list with no synchronization. Hand over a new list each time.

flashcards.front: What does a class need to be immutable?
flashcards.back: All fields `final` and set in the constructor, no setters, changing parts copied in and never handed out, and `this` doesn't escape during construction.

flashcards.front: What does the memory model promise for `final` fields?
flashcards.back: A thread that gets a reference to the object after its constructor finished sees the correct values of its final fields, even without synchronization.

flashcards.front: Is a record with a `List` component immutable?
flashcards.back: Only shallowly. Copy the list in the compact constructor: `items = List.copyOf(items);`.
`unmodifiableList` is a read-only view: the owner's later changes show through. `List.copyOf` is an unmodifiable copy that nobody can change.

flashcards.front: How do you share data that changes rarely, without locks?
flashcards.back: Build a new immutable snapshot, then publish it with one write to a `volatile` field (or an `AtomicReference`). Readers read the reference once.

flashcards.front: A pool thread runs a task that calls `ThreadLocal.set` and never `remove()`. What happens next?
flashcards.back: The value stays on the thread. The next task on that thread sees it if it doesn't set its own.

flashcards.front: What makes passing a changeable object through a `BlockingQueue` safe?
flashcards.back: `put` happens-before `take`, so the taker sees everything done before the put, as long as the giver never touches the object again.

terms.plain: An object whose state can't change after it's built; safe to share without locks.
Copying a changeable argument or return value so nobody else can change your object through it.
Final references to objects that can still change, as in a record holding an `ArrayList`.
Replacing a whole immutable object with one `volatile` write, so readers see one complete version.
Keeping changing state reachable by only one thread.
Passing an object to another thread, through a queue, and never touching it again.
A variable with a separate value per thread; values live as long as the thread unless removed.
A value bound for one call and everything it calls, gone when the call returns (final in JDK 25, JEP 506).

explain_back.prompt: A friend wants to add a lock around the shop's settings (opening hours, prices, offers), which a refresher replaces every minute and every request reads. Explain the alternative you'd suggest, and why it's safe.
explain_back.answer: I'd make the settings an immutable record, with final fields and copied lists, and keep the current one in a `volatile` field. The refresher builds a complete new settings object off to the side and then assigns it to the field in one write. Each request reads the field once and uses that object. It's safe because nothing a reader can reach ever changes. The old object stays valid for whoever is still using it, and the `volatile` write makes the new object, with all its fields, visible to every reader that reads the field afterwards. Readers never wait, and there's no lock to forget. The one thing to watch is a reader that reads the field twice and gets two different versions, so read it into a local first.

deeper.body:
Each `Thread` object keeps its thread-locals in its own small hash map, called `ThreadLocalMap`. The keys are weak references to the `ThreadLocal` objects (references that don't keep an object alive), and the values are ordinary, strong references. When a `ThreadLocal` itself becomes garbage, its key goes away, but the value stays in the map until a later `get`, `set` or `remove` on that thread happens to clean it up. On a pool thread that lives for days, that can be a long time. Servers that load and unload applications while they run know this as a famous leak. A value whose class came from an unloaded application keeps that application's whole class loader, the object that loaded its classes, alive. `remove()` avoids all of it.

`InheritableThreadLocal` copies values from a parent thread to a child thread when the child is created. It does nothing useful with pools, because pool threads are created once, long before the request that hands them work.

Scoped values (JEP 506, final in JDK 25) fix the design problems rather than the symptoms. A binding is immutable: there is no `set`, so code deep in the call chain can't change the value under you. It has a clear lifetime: it ends when `run` or `call` returns, even on an exception. And it is cheap to share with child tasks. With structured concurrency, still a preview API in JDK 25, threads started inside the scope see the same bindings without copying a map per thread.

One immutability trap to know: an object is only safe to share without synchronization if `this` didn't escape while the constructor was running. A constructor that registers `this` as a listener, or starts a thread that uses `this`, hands out the object before its final fields are guaranteed to be visible. Build first, register after. The memory model track's lesson on safe publication covers the full rules.
